triage.reviewer: independent LLM path re-review (Augur IRIS Pass 3, CWE-918 SSRF)
triage.note_on_codeflows: All 3 results carry codeFlows (SARIF threadFlow.locations). Steps carry only ControlFlowNode labels (no per-step source snippets), so each path was independently re-verified against the real Python source at the reported file:line before verdicts were assigned. No diagnostics-query or native-CodeQL-baseline results are present in the SARIF; all 3 results come from queries/Pass3_SSRF.ql only.

source.analysis: `request_url = template_url.async_render(variables=service.data, parse_result=False)` (lines 103-105). The service is registered via `hass.services.async_register(DOMAIN, name, async_service_handler)` (line 154) with NO schema, so any authenticated HA user (non-admin included, via REST POST /api/services or WebSocket) can call rest_command.<name> with an arbitrary data dict; its keys/values become template variables. Source is genuinely attacker-influenced and the entry is reachable. The templateRenderStep summary (argument of .async_render -> render result) matches the real semantics of Template.async_render(variables=...).

sink.api: getattr(websession, method)(request_url, data=..., auth=..., headers=..., timeout=...)
sink.analysis: websession is an aiohttp ClientSession (async_get_clientsession, line 64); method is restricted to get/patch/post/put/delete (SUPPORT_REST_METHODS, line 33, enforced by vol.In in COMMAND_SCHEMA line 40-42). This is a real network request execution, not mere Request-object construction or URL parsing.

findings.taint_path: service.data (line 104, attribute read) --templateRenderStep--> async_render result (line 103) -> request_url (line 103) -> request_url at fetch (line 122). Path is source-supported end to end; the codeFlow in the SARIF matches the real statements.

attacker_control.scope: conditional: bounded by the admin-written YAML URL template
attacker_control.detail: The URL template itself (command_config[CONF_URL], cv.template in COMMAND_SCHEMA line 39) is administrator configuration, not attacker input. The attacker controls only the *values* substituted for template variables. If the template interpolates a variable into scheme/host position (e.g. '{{ url }}' or '{{ scheme }}://{{ host }}/...'), the attacker gets full host/port/path control (true SSRF); if variables appear only in path/query, control is path-only on a fixed host. Both shapes are legal rest_command configurations, so exploitability is config-dependent.
attacker_control.entry: any authenticated HA user; REST APIDomainServicesView / WebSocket service call; no admin gate, no service schema.

findings.url_transforms: None. No urljoin / base-URL / yarl.URL normalization is applied to the rendered URL before the fetch; the rendered string is passed verbatim.

guards.note: No sanitizer on this path. cv.template validates only that config values are templates; there is no cv.url, no is_allowed_external_url, no scheme allow-list. Template variables from service.data are unrestricted (no service schema).

findings.trusted_fixed_url_check: The URL *template* is admin config, but the rendered URL embeds attacker-controlled variable values, so this is not a fixed-destination fetch.
findings.static_reachability: Real: async_setup -> async_register_rest_command (line 156-157, iterates YAML config) -> service registration (line 154) -> async_service_handler on every service call. Precondition: the rest_command integration is configured in configuration.yaml (setup-only condition, not a permission barrier).
findings.file_or_test_check: Not file:/local read, not URL-parsing-only, not test code, not a diagnostics result. Runtime component code.
findings.rationale: Source (authenticated service-call data, no schema), propagation (template render with variables=service.data), and sink (aiohttp session request) are all real and unmitigated. The only caveat is that host-level control requires the admin template to place a variable in scheme/host position, which is a configuration-dependent exploitability condition rather than a data-flow error. Under the reviewed threat model (service_data family is a labeled tp source family: 'reachable by any authenticated HA user'), this is a likely true positive.

source.analysis: `url = service.data[ATTR_URL]` inside download_file service handler (line 61). Service `downloader.download_file` is registered at lines 169-174 with SERVICE_DOWNLOAD_FILE_SCHEMA: vol.Required('url'): cv.url. cv.url is a URL-shape check only (voluptuous URL validation) - it does not restrict scheme to http/https, does not restrict host, and is documented in the labels as non-sanitizing. Entry: any authenticated HA user via REST/WebSocket service call; no admin gate.

sink.analysis: Synchronous requests.get - a real server-side HTTP fetch, executed in a worker thread (threading.Thread(target=do_download), line 167). The response body is written to the local filesystem (lines 136-138). This is a full outbound request + response capture, not Request-object creation or URL parsing.

findings.taint_path: service.data (line 67, attribute read) -> url (line 67) -> url at requests.get (line 81). Direct assignment, no intermediate transforms; both codeFlows in the SARIF are identical copies of this single real path.

attacker_control.scope: full URL (host, port, path, query) - strongest form
attacker_control.detail: The attacker supplies the entire url string. requests only performs http/https (file:// etc. raise InvalidSchema), and requests follows redirects by default, so even a 'safe-looking' external URL can bounce to internal hosts. Port and path fully controlled. Response content is persisted to disk with an attacker-influenced filename (guarded by raise_if_invalid_filename, line 108) - the SSRF primitive itself (internal network reachability, internal GET/redirect-chain) is unmitigated.

findings.url_transforms: None. The url string is passed verbatim to requests.get; no urljoin, no base URL, no yarl normalization.

guards.scheme_validation: partial - cv.url requires a URL *shape* (scheme present), but permits any scheme string; effective scheme restriction comes only from requests' internal http/https-only handling, which does not restrict host.
guards.note: is_allowed_external_url is NOT applied on this path (the sanitizer is modeled only at color_extractor/discord/slack/signal_messenger sites). raise_if_invalid_path / raise_if_invalid_filename (lines 77, 108) guard the *output file path*, not the request URL.

findings.trusted_fixed_url_check: No. Destination is fully attacker-chosen per call; this is not a config-fixed endpoint.
findings.static_reachability: Real: setup (line 46) requires the downloader integration to be configured with an existing download_dir (YAML precondition); once set up, the service is callable by any authenticated user and the handler runs on each call.
findings.file_or_test_check: Not file: read, not URL-parse-only, not test code, not diagnostics. Runtime component code. (The component does also write the response to a local file, but the flagged data flow is the network fetch itself, which is genuine.)
findings.rationale: Textbook authenticated-user SSRF: unvalidated full-URL service field -> server-side requests.get -> response saved to disk. Source, propagation and sink all verified in source. The only preconditions are integration setup and an authenticated (non-admin) account, consistent with the reviewed service_data threat model.

source.analysis: In _handle_websocket: `url = self._create_url(token, path)` (line 126) then `if request.query_string: url = f"{url}?{request.query_string}"` (line 131). The flagged source is request.query_string - a genuine attacker-supplied request attribute. The view HassIOIngress (url '/api/hassio_ingress/{token}/{path:.*}', line 61) has requires_auth=False, so the HTTP entry itself is unauthenticated; the effective access control is the ingress token, a long random supervisor-issued secret.

sink.analysis: Real aiohttp websocket connection. The sink is a genuine network request, so the question is purely about destination control.

findings.taint_path: request.query_string (line 131:28) -> url (line 131:13) -> url at ws_connect (line 135:13). The path is real as data flow; the question is whether it constitutes SSRF.

attacker_control.scope: query string (and, via the route, the {path:.*} segment) only; host/port/scheme are fixed
attacker_control.detail: The destination is always `http://{self._host}/ingress/{token}/{quote(path)}` (_create_url, lines 70-81): fixed supervisor host (self._host set at async_setup_ingress, line 49), fixed http scheme, fixed port. The attacker cannot change the target host, port, or protocol - only the path below /ingress/{token}/ and the query string. This is the designed ingress reverse-proxy behavior (forwarding a browser's request to the add-on's ingress endpoint), not a forged destination.

findings.url_transforms: The URL is constructed by f-string with quote(path); _create_url additionally re-parses with yarl and enforces `URL(url).path.startswith(base_path)` where base_path = f"/ingress/{token}/" (lines 75-79), rejecting paths whose normalized form escapes the ingress prefix (dot-segment traversal). The query_string is appended verbatim, but only as a query component - it cannot alter host.

guards.scheme_validation: implicit - scheme is the literal 'http' in the f-string, not attacker-influenced
guards.host_allowlist: fixed host by construction (supervisor address from the hassio setup)
guards.redirect_recheck: allow_redirects=False on the plain-HTTP sibling path (_handle_request, line 164); the flagged ws_connect path does not follow redirects
guards.access_control: requires_auth=False but a valid supervisor-issued ingress token (bearer-style random secret) is required to hit a meaningful target

findings.trusted_fixed_url_check: Yes in the sense that matters: the destination host is the local supervisor, and proxying arbitrary paths/queries to the add-on behind the presented token is the component's documented function. It is not an admin-config address but a fixed internal service endpoint.
findings.static_reachability: Real (view registered at line 54; get/post/put/delete/patch/options all route to _handle, lines 100-105; websocket upgrade detection at line 89). Reachability is not in dispute; the dispute is classification.
findings.file_or_test_check: Not file:, not parse-only, not test code, not diagnostics. Runtime component code.
findings.rationale: Although the data flow request.query_string -> ws_connect(url) is technically real, the attacker controls neither scheme, host, nor port - the request always targets the fixed local supervisor ingress endpoint for the token already presented by the same requester, with a path-prefix normalization guard and (on the HTTP variant) redirects disabled. This is the intended ingress proxy feature, not SSRF: there is no capability the attacker gains beyond what the ingress token already authorizes. The alert's own scope string concedes 'fixed supervisor host; attacker controls only path/query'. Marked likely_fp under criterion 5/7 (fixed destination, limited attacker-controlled parameters, by-design resource loading).

ground_truth_cross_check.question: Was the real vulnerability (commit e0eb63c58816818530ccda4e9bf0069bba58ed5c, 'Validate slug in addon services', CWE-918, function send_command) localized by this analysis?

vulnerable_call_chain: homeassistant/components/hassio/__init__.py:490 - data = service.data.copy() (attacker data, any authenticated user)
homeassistant/components/hassio/__init__.py:491 - addon = data.pop(ATTR_ADDON, None) -- SCHEMA_ADDON (line 154) validates addon only as cv.string: NO slug validation (the fix adds it)

homeassistant/components/hassio/__init__.py:508-513 - hassio.send_command(api_endpoint.command.format(addon=addon, slug=slug), payload=data[ATTR_INPUT], ...) -- attacker controls both the {addon} path segment and the JSON payload

homeassistant/components/hassio/handler.py:533-537 - self.websession.request(method, f"http://{self._ip}{command}", json=payload, ...) -- path injection into the supervisor REST URL (fixed host) with attacker-controlled POST body
real_vulnerability.snapshot_vs_fix: DB snapshot git e2dd7f2 (2023-08-29) predates fix commit e0eb63c (#99232, 'Validate slug in addon services'): SCHEMA_ADDON still uses cv.string and send_command has no `url != str(URL(url))` normalization check, i.e. the pre-fix vulnerable code is exactly what the database was built from.
real_vulnerability.impact: An authenticated attacker calling hassio.addon_stdin with a crafted addon value (e.g. containing '../' segments) can invoke arbitrary Supervisor REST endpoints via POST with a fully attacker-controlled data dictionary.

detection_outcome.detail: The 3 formal py/augur/core/pass3-ssrf alerts are rest_command:122, downloader:81, and hassio/ingress.py:135. None is located in homeassistant/components/hassio/__init__.py or hassio/handler.py; no alert covers the addon_stdin -> send_command path.
root_cause_of_miss: Sink excluded at labeling: label p3-snk-3724 (role none, classification fp, confidence 0.75) pinned handler.py:534 'websession.request' with rationale 'supervisor API funnel: f-string http://{self._ip}{command} with FIXED supervisor host and internal command strings.' The 'internal command strings' assumption is wrong for the addon/slug services: command is a template '/addons/{addon}/stdin' formatted with attacker-supplied service data (line 512-513), so the command path IS attacker-influenced. This is exactly the fixed-host/path-injection pattern the real CVE exploits.

Wrapper excluded: label p3-snk-3894 (role none, fp, 0.7) treats send_command as a fetch wrapper ('the wrapper itself issues no request'), relying on inter-procedural flow to the inner sink - but the inner sink was itself excluded by p3-snk-3724, so the chain terminates.

Source side was correctly captured: label p3-src-1674 (source, tp, 0.8) at hassio/__init__.py:490 for the service.data read. The miss is entirely on the sink side, plus the unmodeled `command.format(addon=addon, slug=slug)` string-format step which would additionally impede flow even with the sink present.
detection_outcome.consistency_note: The pass-3 model *did* report the structurally analogous fixed-host/path-only pattern at hassio/ingress.py:135 (as a candidate), while the identical-shape but genuinely vulnerable fixed-host path-injection at hassio/handler.py:534 was explicitly filtered as fp at label time. The real CVE lives in the excluded site, not in the reported one.

ground_truth_cross_check.conclusion: The formal Augur Pass 3 results did NOT localize the ground-truth CWE-918 vulnerability (hassio.addon_stdin -> HassIO.send_command). The miss was caused by a Phase 1 labeling decision (p3-snk-3724 / p3-snk-3894, 'fixed supervisor host and internal command strings'), not by a query-execution or path-resolution failure; the source label for the same path (p3-src-1674) was correct. Detection would have required (a) keeping handler.py:534 as a host-fixed/path-tainted sink and (b) a taint step for str.format with keyword/positional arguments.
